tasks.intent: Show how life expectancy relates to GDP per capita across countries for the most recent year, and whether the relationship flattens at high incomes.

data.description: One recent year of national life expectancy at birth paired with GDP per capita (PPP, constant international-$) for ~180 countries, with population available for point sizing and world region for grouping.
data.shape: ~180 countries x 2 quantitative (GDP per capita, life expectancy) + 1 quantitative for size (population) + 1 categorical (region)

expected.chart_family: scatterplot with logarithmic x-axis (GDP per capita), optionally bubble-sized by population and colored by region
expected.key_insight: Life expectancy rises steeply with income at low GDP and then saturates — the Preston-curve concavity that only reads correctly once income is on a log scale.

failure_modes: plotting GDP per capita on a linear x-axis, which crushes 150 poor countries into the left margin and hides the concave saturation Cleveland's position-along-a-common-scale judgment depends on
connecting the points with a line as if the cross-section were a time series, manufacturing a nonexistent trajectory through unordered countries
encoding population by bubble diameter instead of area, so a country with 4x the population looks 16x larger and overstates the big nations (Tufte lie factor)
a rainbow region palette that assigns maximally saturated hues at random, forcing serial visual search instead of letting continents pop out as Gestalt groups
hiding the log transform without an annotation or gridline labels, so a reader mistakes the flattening curve for a linear ceiling

tasks.intent: Is a country's adult obesity prevalence associated with its per-capita daily calorie supply? Plot the two against each other for the latest available year.

data.description: Latest-year national adult obesity prevalence (% of adults with BMI >= 30) paired with daily per-capita dietary energy supply (kcal/person/day) across ~170 countries.
data.shape: ~170 countries x 2 quantitative (kcal supply, obesity prevalence)

expected.chart_family: scatterplot with a robust (LOWESS or linear) trend line and shaded confidence band
expected.key_insight: A positive but noisy association — higher calorie supply tracks higher obesity, but the scatter is wide enough that supply alone is a weak predictor, which the spread should make visually honest.

failure_modes: reducing 170 countries to a single correlation coefficient printed on an empty panel, discarding the scatter that reveals outliers and heteroscedasticity (anti-Anscombe)
drawing a bar chart of obesity ranked by country, which answers 'who is highest' but destroys the two-variable relationship the ask is about
extrapolating the trend line past the data cloud to the axis origin, implying a prediction where no observations exist
using a dark-on-dark or low-contrast point color that fails WCAG contrast against the plot background, so dense clusters become an unreadable smear
overplotting hundreds of opaque markers with no transparency or jitter, hiding density where countries pile up

tasks.intent: Across countries, does higher annual per-capita CO2 emissions go with higher GDP per capita? Show the recent-year relationship.

data.description: Recent-year national per-capita CO2 emissions (tonnes/person) paired with GDP per capita (PPP, constant international-$) for ~180 countries, with region available for coloring.
data.shape: ~180 countries x 2 quantitative (GDP per capita, CO2 per capita) + 1 categorical (region)

expected.chart_family: scatterplot on log-log axes with a fitted power-law slope, colored by region
expected.key_insight: A near-linear positive relationship on log-log axes — emissions scale with income as a power law — with a handful of oil-economy and low-carbon-grid outliers sitting off the main band.

failure_modes: linear-linear axes that compress the poorest 120 countries into a corner and let a few high-emission petrostates dominate the whole frame
dual y-axes plotting CO2 and GDP as two separate series against country index, inviting a spurious eyeballed correlation from arbitrary axis alignment (Tufte's dual-axis warning)
a sequential single-hue ramp used to encode the unordered categorical 'region', misapplying an ordered color scale to a nominal variable (Bertin selective vs ordered)
labeling every one of 180 points, producing a wall of overlapping text that buries the signal instead of annotating only the informative outliers
omitting units on the axes so a reader cannot tell tonnes from kilograms or PPP from nominal dollars

tasks.intent: For US states, is median household income related to the share of adults with a bachelor's degree or higher? Plot one against the other.

data.description: Most recent ACS 1-year estimates by state: median household income (US$) paired with the percentage of adults 25+ holding a bachelor's degree or higher, 50 states plus DC.
data.shape: 51 states x 2 quantitative (educational attainment %, median household income)

expected.chart_family: scatterplot with direct point labels for notable states and a linear trend line
expected.key_insight: A strong positive association between the college-educated share and median income, with a clear regression slope and a few high-cost or resource-economy states departing from the line.

failure_modes: a truncated income y-axis starting at $50k that visually inflates the spread between states and exaggerates how steep the relationship is (Tufte lie factor)
state abbreviations rendered as a legend keyed by marker color across 51 categories, an impossible color-matching task instead of direct labeling
a grouped or clustered bar chart per state, which encodes two variables as adjacent bars and defeats the point of showing their covariation
computing income in nominal dollars without noting cost-of-living, then reading the raw slope as a causal return to education in the annotation
a background gridline density so heavy that the data points recede — non-data ink dominating the plot (Tufte data-ink ratio)

tasks.intent: Across countries, does greater electricity consumption per capita come with a higher share of the population having internet access? Show the relationship for the latest year.

data.description: Latest-year national electric power consumption per capita (kWh/person) paired with the share of individuals using the internet (% of population), ~150 countries, with income group available for grouping.
data.shape: ~150 countries x 2 quantitative (electricity per capita, internet use %) + 1 categorical (income group)

expected.chart_family: scatterplot with a logarithmic x-axis (electricity per capita), colored by World Bank income group
expected.key_insight: A saturating positive relationship — internet adoption climbs sharply with electricity access at low consumption and plateaus near 100% for high-consumption countries, a ceiling effect visible only on a log x-axis.

failure_modes: a linear electricity axis that piles low-consumption countries against the y-axis and hides the sharp early rise, defeating the position-on-common-scale comparison

a rainbow (spectral) palette mapped to the ordered income groups, so the reader cannot tell low- from high-income order because hue carries no natural magnitude ranking (Ware / Bertin ordered encoding)
letting the internet-share axis exceed 100% or run negative because auto-scaling ignored the variable's natural [0,100] bounds
connecting the country points into a line, imposing a false continuous trajectory on an unordered cross-section
encoding income group redundantly by both hue and marker shape while omitting the legend, so neither channel is decodable
